paragraphs: Fate. Choice. Free will and destiny. A non-linear novel with deep philosophical undertones, this book explores the different possibilities that are, could be, could have been, could never have been; in the life of the protagonist. Although, personality itself a product of different and unique timelines, perhaps I should say protagonists. Four lives, one character. One origin. Time, circumstance, happenstance, coincidence – all inevitably leading to that which never could have been, and that which is.

An excellent, thoroughly researched review concerning the issues facing Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) today, and some of the potential fixes for tomorrow. Issues limited not just to technical limitations, but more importantly, to social issues such as with hiring, justice, policing, health, and many more. This book provides not only great insights into the functioning of the black-boxes that are ML models, but also provides insights into how humans learn. Touches on philosophy, psychology and neuroscience as much as it touches on computer science and engineering.

This book takes psychological and physical conditioning to its logical extreme. A humorous-at-first presentation of a society that has its different echelons hard-coded and generated, with emotional control through a drug called Soma, this book explores a dystopian future where it takes the contemporary classification of society to an extreme. The segment of humanity that lives outside of this conditioning has been relegated to the borderlines of this society, and the protagonist faces a clash between the two.

Books being burnt by the Authority, the protagonist - himself a book-burning employee of the Authority - steals and reads a book. With this event follows a murder, a manhunt, another murder, and unrelatedly (or perhaps relatedly), the destuction of his city. With the rise of social media and the decline of the book-reading population, this book may be more relevant today then when it was during the rise of TV dinners-on-a-tray. With the current censorship of media in the form of allowing certain narratives to reign over other minority voices, this book warns us of a future that already may be all too near.

This book, as the title indicates, talks about interpretation. It argues that everything is a matter of interpretation, and that without an angle of interpretation, it would be impossible to understand anything. It discusses Heidegger and Derrida, amongst other philosophers, and controversies and ideas surrounding them. Without giving much away, my interpretation is that it takes a post-modern relativist approach to modern hermeneutics.

To those reading about how science and religion are incompatible (Hawking and Dawkins, just to name a couple), I have this message for you: use your intellect and read this book. Those authors were writing from a particular religiuos canon (which I will not name), yet Islam - the true religion - poses no such incompatibility. Cosmology, evolution, you name it. The Holy Qur'an both supports and reinforces such scientific thought. Have a look, if you're intellectually curious enough!

page_title: Never Split the Difference - Chris Voss and Tahl Raz
review_heading: Never Split the Difference - Book Review
paragraphs: Contains tons of strategies to help you in the art of negotiation. Speaking from his personal experience as a professional hostage negotiator, the author translates his experience into actionable knowledge you can use to your advantage in any situation: whether while shopping, at work, in business, or anywhere in your life.

page_title: The Psychology of Money - Morgan Housel
review_heading: The Psychology of Money - Book Review
paragraphs: To understand money, you need psychology more than you need mathematics – this is what the book expounds. Financial decisions, as the book claims, are made with emotions rather than pure logic. This principle helps one understand poor, and good, economic actions. As the books says, financial success is not a hard science but more of a soft skill – behavior being more important than what you think you know. Each chapter then goes on to treat different aspects of behavioral finance (as I call it), from surviving to thriving.

Shoe Dog is the memoir of Phil Knight, the founder of Nike. This book offers proof that the path to (business) success is rarely short, linear, or easy. Phil Knight testifies to the amount of struggle and patience it can take to generate such success. I found this book a moving and insightful read, and I highly recommend it to anyone who is interested in entrepreneurship or business.

I really recommend reading this book as it goes into to what drives success and what drives people to follow you - the short answer is, it’s your own motivation to do what you do. Having a clear sense of WHY is the discriminant between exceptionality and mediocrity, as the book expounds upon with several examples from both the business world and beyond. A must-read for anyone after any kind of entrepreneurial, leadership, influential, or more generally-defined success.

page_title: The stuff of thought - Steven Pinker
review_heading: The Stuff of Thought - Book Review
paragraphs: Though the book is sub-titled "Language as a window into human nature," this book really should be titled "the English language as a window into anglophonic nature." Given that this book studies the English language only, the author should not advertise that his conclusions generalise to other languages (though he does acknowledge this limitation in a way within the text). Indeed, though language affects thought and thought affects human nature, the kind of human nature proposed to be understood through this book is only very specific to the minds of English-language speakers (see also my upcoming piece on the relation between language and philosophy). However, this book does a good job at that specific task.
